source: I still don't know how he died. The letter didn't mention more than his murder. Though I have my suspicions.
A blackhearted rumor floats around town, my lord. I'd desire you to hear it from a kind voice first. Your sister, perhaps.
You and I are brothers of a kind. What is this vile rumor?
The people whisper he was murdered, my lord. By the King's hand.
I see. Somehow I can't find it in me to be surprised.
Here I assumed that bastard Hamlet would have done the deed. But the King is his blood, and murderers tend to generate more of their kind.
With the bastard dead, it's too bad there's no one to ask about it.
Lord Laertes... it always was a funny title.
What fortunate luck that our ship was delayed in its leave of harbor.
The letter I received spoke of something horrible.
Prince Hamlet made an attempt on my father's life. And now I must repay the deed in kind.
Any honorable man would surely feel the same, my lord.
Though the precise interpretation of 'repaying the deed' is subject to some discussion, I should think.
After all, the Prince is dead.
He-- Hamlet-- is dead?
Yes. It came as a surprise to me, too.
Can you not bring him to justice?
Perhaps. But as things stand, I desire only his death and my family's immediate safety.
I have to believe Claudius was behind this somehow. That he ordered Hamlet to come after my father.
Hamlet may be a fool, but he wouldn't plot against my father alone. Not without being... pushed.
The letter spoke only of 'urgent matters' requiring my attention back at home.
Ah. That'll likely be the Prince, rest his soul.
I... I see.
I suppose woes spring forth other woes wherever they might land. And I sense more are soon to follow.
Speaking of springing forth... I've heard that Prince Hamlet and Lady Birgitta are to be wed soon.
Wed? You cannot be serious!
It's a new brand of gossip, my lord, but I believe it trustworthy.
The servants who wait upon them both bring swift news to my bar-top.
Brit... marrying him?
Of course the second I depart, Hamlet plots to make her his.
The bastard.
Ah, and have you heard the news regarding King Claudius, my lord?
He is dead.
Well, that's certainly news.
And what is to become of the throne, then?
They whisper that Hamlet shall rule now.
What? That incompetent boy?
Not if I can help it.
I have heard nothing yet, my lord.
How can all this have taken place in just two days' time?
I, too, am continually surprised. You Danes are an awfully busy, bloody sort, aren't you.
Although I don't know you well, I wish you fortune in whatever you may find when you make your return.
And I welcome it. I've really no idea what's happening. I suppose I'll soon find out.
... Look at me.
Not half a day back from France and all I can think about is murder. The longer I must linger among awful men...
The closer I grow to them. Well, fine, then. Let it suit my bloody purpose.
It's time. I should have been King. The post was always rightfully mine.
Hamlet's mad, the people always hated Claudius... Who better than myself to rule?
Time to take what belongs to me.
My lord, a letter arrives from Hamlet by pigeon.
H—Hamlet? Good captain, I must have misheard you—surely?
Forgive me, my lord, I'm as surprised as you. He ought to be in England by now!
C-certainly so. What does it say?
It says he's returning to Denmark. And his ship was overtaken by... pirates?
Not one day at sea and they were beset by pirates?
Stranger still, those same pirates are helping him return to Denmark.
Pah! This is preposterous! Bernardo, can you believe this?
Knowing Hamlet, I absolutely can, my lord.
The letter goes on to say that Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are dead.
That's a shame.
This is terrible, terrible news...
Indeed, my lord. I know they were dear friends of Hamlet's.
No—not that, you idiot! Out with you! Everyone, out!
Indeed, my lord. But perhaps Hamlet will convalesce better at home.
You have crossed the line. The people hate you, as do I.
My ship, delayed by mishap, returned to harbor...
And the moment I stepped ashore, I learned my father was slain.
Who else would have arranged his death other than you? You never trusted him—and I knew it to be true.
Soon I will rally more men to knock at your gates. It's time for a new King.
Denmark calls out for blood, and the blood of my father must answer!
Wait! This is about your father?
My father's death is on your head. Murdering the man who trusted and defended you most? That's sick, Claudius.
W-wait! Don't act just yet! You must know the truth!
The truth? Spit it out.
Hamlet killed my father due to your negligence. You noticed the signs of his madness. We all did.
And yet you sent him, a dog unchained, to run in my father's path and bite him. You might as well have laid the killing blow!
I never laid a hand on your father. It was Hamlet who killed him, of his own volition.
And you had no indirect involvement?
No. None whatsoever.
If you want proof, ask Hamlet himself!
How could Hamlet have acted alone?
Had something changed in him?
(Of course, I know all this is true already.)
(But Hamlet's grief is as deep as mine. He regrets what he did.)
(Still, I must act as though I am true to Claudius.)
Laertes. Listen, boy. I had no hand in your father's death.
Hamlet intended to kill him and struck the killing blow. I wasn't even present for your father's death... much to my regret.
I will forever wish I could have saved him. He was a fine advisor, the best I ever saw in Denmark.
Hamlet isn't here to answer for the truth of your word, Claudius.
He returns to Denmark anon. We've received word of his return. Patience, Laertes. Patience is a true virtue for a man of your age.
Ask anyone in Elsinore, and they shall tell you the truth of what happened that night.
If you receive any other answer, then you may rally against me. But you won't. Patience is a true virtue for a man of your age, you know.
Be patient, and it will richly reward you. Of that, I am certain.
Let me help you achieve your goals, Laertes. They are mine, too.
How can I trust you? You're his uncle. What's to stop you from lying to me?
I'll give you the very weapon to gut him with.
I had poison I could dip the blade in—only a single nick would have been needed to rid him.
It has been... misplaced.
But you are unparalleled as a swordsman. Your skill is demonstrable. You will prevail.
I have in my chambers a certain... set of tools, poison amongst the most useful.
I shall apply it to one of my sharpest blades. All you need do is nick him a single time and he'll be dead for good.
Barring that, I'll lay a few drops upon the rim of a wine goblet. If the duel comes to a draw, I'll offer the wine to him as a blessing.
Our two problems, intertwined, solved all at once.
(My word to Hamlet, that is. Your hourglass trickles down, Claudius.)
I will await this blade, Claudius. Make good on your word, and I'll make good on mine.
Everyone left rather hastily, it seems.
I ought to go find out where the others went.
Ah, but it's about the hour when last time...
Well, there's no use in crying out. I won't be heard.
Wish they wouldn't all turn heel on a moment's notice.
Who's there?
I am sorry for what I must do.
W-who are you?
For whatever little it's worth, you are innocent of this matter.
Denmark as it stands now must fall. It must fall. And you are the lamb whose blood must be spilled.
So you're the spy the King warned about. You are real.
The King is so abjectly useless, he cannot even whiff out an enemy in his own court.
The King is so abjectly useless, he cannot even whiff out a spy in his own court.
Y-you've been spying on us? On me? What do you intend to do?
But it has fallen. Claudius is dead. What more could my death offer?
Your continued existence, by its very nature, poses a threat to long-laid plans.
I didn't want to hurt you. Not really.
They'll never know about this, of course. They'll think you drowned in the end, the louts.
I feel my body growing cold.

source: I've got a feeling I'm about to be 'accosted' again.
Stay your hand a moment. I need to talk to you.
Who are you? Why are you doing this? What do you want?
I'm sorry.
Denmark must fall. It must fall. And you are the lamb whose blood must be spilled.
How does my death play into Denmark's fall? I am no one to you.
To me, you are nothing. But you are an important person to important people. And that makes you useful.
(I failed to stop it again.)
Help! Someone, please—
Fine. Do what you will. But I will find you, and uncover your crime. This will end.
Do it quickly.
A piece in someone's larger schemes.

source: Lady Brit.
I knew it. You may kill me now, but I know everything I need to know.
Just wait. I know I'll succeed in stopping you.
Shut up! Just--die! I have to do this!
A piece in her larger schemes.

source: Ah. Ophelia. Convenient to run into you.
Where are you off to?
Hamlet's returned, against all odds. He sent word to me to meet him. He did ask for you, too.
Though I wasn't certain I'd find you, or that you'd want to see him even if I did.
He's not in England?
Something's gone horribly wrong, though I know not what.
Heed Hamlet's request?

source: No, Horatio. You meet him alone. I'll not go.
For better or for worse, I have returned.
Of course, I trust things have fared excellently in my absence.
It's certainly been... quiet, if nothing else. A little too still.
Good. Things are about to awaken once more.
My dear uncle wants me murdered, just as he did my father.
I beg your pardon?
I uncovered his treachery nearly the moment we set sail. I had a sneaking feeling something was amiss.
He sent a note along with Rosencrantz and Guildenstern to the Queen of England, ordering her to hang me upon arrival.
F-for what reason?
In the interest of 'betterment' of our two nations' friendship, or some sort of rubbish of that nature.
I must believe Rosencrantz and Guildenstern intended to bear this letter to England and carry out these orders at my uncle's behest.
I thought them my friends. More the fool am I.
